questions.topic: Light: dispersion - deviation of different colours in glass
questions.question: When light enters from air to glass, it bends toward the normal. If red, blue, and yellow colours are allowed to enter the same glass block at the same angle of incidence, then for which colour, the value of ∠i − ∠r, be greater?

options.a: green
options.b: red
options.c: blue
options.d: yellow

questions.solution: (c) blue. Glass has the greatest refractive index for blue light (shorter wavelength), so for the same ∠i the angle of refraction ∠r is smallest for blue; hence the deviation ∠i − ∠r is greatest for blue.

questions.topic: Light: deviation through a prism, principle of reversibility
concepts: same deviation for two angles of incidence
questions.question:
Assertion (A): When light passes through a triangular prism, it is observed that for two angles of incidence, the angle of deviation is the same.
Reason (R): According to the principle of reversibility, the light retraces the path in reversing the direction.

options.a: A and R are true, and R is the reason for A.
options.b: A and R are true, and R is not the reason for A.
options.c: A is true, but R is false.
options.d: A is false, but R is true.

questions.solution: (a) A and R are true, and R is the reason for A. By the principle of reversibility, if a ray incident at angle i emerges at angle e, a ray incident at angle e will emerge at angle i with the same deviation. So (except at minimum deviation, where i = e) two different angles of incidence give the same deviation.

questions.topic: Light: ray diagrams for lenses (oblique rays)
concepts: oblique parallel rays meet on the focal plane
questions.question: Which of the following diagrams shows the correct path of light through the lens?

options.a: Convex lens: a ray parallel to the axis emerges diverging, as if coming from F on the incident side
options.b: Concave lens: an oblique ray emerges diverging, appearing to come from the point where the parallel line through the optical centre meets the first focal plane
options.c: Convex lens: a beam of oblique parallel rays converges at the principal focus F on the axis
options.d: Concave lens: a ray parallel to the axis bends and passes through F on the other side

questions.solution: (b) The concave-lens diagram. An oblique ray incident on a concave lens emerges diverging, as if coming from the point where a line drawn through the optical centre parallel to the incident ray meets the first focal plane — exactly what (b) shows. (a) is wrong: a convex lens converges a parallel ray through the second focus. (c) is wrong: oblique parallel rays converge to a point on the focal plane off the axis, not at F. (d) is wrong: a concave lens cannot converge a parallel ray through F.
questions.figure_desc: Four ray diagrams (a)-(d): two convex and two concave lenses with 2F and F marked, showing different refracted ray paths.

questions.topic: Force, Work, Power and Energy: velocity ratio of pulley systems
concepts: V.R. = number of strands supporting the movable block
questions.question: The diagrams below show four pulley systems. State which of the statements following the diagrams is true.

options.a: There are three pulley systems with V.R. = 2 and one pulley system with V.R. = 1.
options.b: There are two pulley systems with V.R. = 2, one pulley system with V.R. = 3 and one pulley system with V.R. = 1.
options.c: There are two pulley systems with V.R. = 2, one pulley system with V.R. = 3 and one pulley system with V.R. = 4.
options.d: There are two pulley systems with V.R. = 2 and two pulley systems with V.R. = 3.

questions.solution: (d) There are two pulley systems with V.R. = 2 and two pulley systems with V.R. = 3. V.R. equals the number of rope segments supporting the movable block: single movable pulley with effort upward = 2; movable + fixed pulley with effort downward = 2; the two-pulley system with the rope tied to the lower block and effort pulled up = 3; the block and tackle with two pulleys above and one below (rope tied to the lower block) = 3.
questions.figure_desc: Four pulley arrangements: a fixed+movable pair with rope tied to the lower block (effort up), a single movable pulley (effort up), a block and tackle with two upper and one lower pulley, and a movable pulley with a fixed pulley (effort down).

questions.chapter: Force: Turning Forces and Uniform Circular Motion
questions.topic: Force, Work, Power and Energy: moment of force and direction of force
questions.question:
The diagrams below show a force F = 40 N acting on a rod AB (length 80 cm) pivoted at A in different directions. Identify the correct statement.
(P: F acts vertically upward at B; Q: F acts vertically downward at B; R and S: F acts obliquely at B.)

options.a: P and S have opposite moments.
options.b: The magnitude of the moment of force is maximum in R.
options.c: The magnitude of the moment of force is maximum in P and Q.
options.d: The moment of force in R is negative.

questions.solution: (c) The magnitude of the moment of force is maximum in P and Q. In P and Q the force is perpendicular to the rod, so moment = 40 × 0.8 = 32 N m (P anticlockwise, Q clockwise). In R and S the force is oblique, so the perpendicular distance from A is less than 0.8 m and the moment is smaller.
questions.figure_desc: Four sketches P, Q, R, S of an 80 cm rod AB pivoted at A with a 40 N force at B acting up (P), down (Q), and obliquely (R, S).

questions.chapter: Force: Turning Forces and Uniform Circular Motion
questions.topic: Force, Work, Power and Energy: centre of gravity of a solid cone
concepts: C.G. of solid cone at h/4 from base
questions.question: In the diagram, four cones are depicted, each with a height of 12 cm. The position of the centre of gravity is indicated by dots located at 9 cm, 8 cm, 4 cm, and 3 cm from the apex of each cone. Which of these cones is completely solid?

options.a: 9 cm
options.b: 8 cm
options.c: 4 cm
options.d: 3 cm

questions.solution: (a) 9 cm. The C.G. of a solid cone lies on its axis at h/4 from the base = 12/4 = 3 cm from the base, i.e. 12 − 3 = 9 cm from the apex.

questions.topic: Force, Work, Power and Energy: work done by a force at an angle (graph)
questions.question:
The given figure depicts the graph of work done vs. displacement under a constant force of 10 N. Which of the following statements is true?
(The graph is a straight line through the origin; work done = 200 J at a displacement of 40 m.)

options.a: Force is acting at an angle of 0° with the displacement.
options.b: Force is acting at an angle of 45° with the displacement.
options.c: Force is acting at an angle of 60° with the displacement.
options.d: Force is acting at an angle of 90° with the displacement.

questions.solution: (c) Force is acting at an angle of 60° with the displacement. W = F s cos θ ⇒ 200 = 10 × 40 × cos θ ⇒ cos θ = 0.5 ⇒ θ = 60°.

questions.topic: Force, Work, Power and Energy: effect of friction on effort, M.A. and efficiency
questions.question: During his experiments with a single movable pulley, Jas determined the effort, mechanical advantage and efficiency as X, Y & Z, respectively. Subsequently, after lubricating the pulley thoroughly, he recalculated the effort, MA and efficiency as X', Y' & Z' respectively. Which of the following relationships accurately represents the scenario?

options.a: X' > X
options.b: Y' < Y
options.c: Z' > Z
options.d: Z' = Z

questions.solution: (c) Z' > Z. Lubrication reduces friction, so less effort is needed (X' < X), M.A. increases (Y' > Y) and, since V.R. is unchanged, efficiency = M.A./V.R. increases (Z' > Z).

questions.topic: Light: Snell's law and the i vs r graph
concepts: Snell's law: sin i / sin r = constant
i vs r graph is not linear
questions.question:
Assertion (A): For a glass block, the i vs. r graph is a straight line.
Reason (R): When a ray of light undergoes refraction, it follows Snell's law.

options.a: Both Assertion and Reason are true, and the Reason is the correct explanation of the Assertion.
options.b: Both Assertion and Reason are true, but Reason is not the correct explanation of the Assertion.
options.c: Assertion is true, but the Reason is false.
options.d: Assertion is false, but the Reason is true.

questions.solution: (d) Assertion is false, but the Reason is true. Snell's law says sin i / sin r is constant, not i / r; so the sin i vs sin r graph is a straight line, while the i vs r graph is a curve.

questions.topic: Sound (as printed): electromagnetic spectrum - UV vs microwaves
concepts: UV has higher frequency than microwaves
all e.m. waves have the same speed in vacuum
questions.question:
________ of UV > ________ of microwaves
The quantity suitable for filling in both the blanks is:

options.a: speed in vacuum
options.b: speed in a medium
options.c: frequency
options.d: wavelength

questions.solution: (c) frequency. UV radiation has a much higher frequency (and shorter wavelength) than microwaves; both travel at the same speed in vacuum.

questions.topic: Sound: loudness and amplitude
questions.question:
Sumit, a teenager, enjoys playing his music loudly. However, his grandmother consistently lowers the volume of the music player. Analyse the wave to identify which characteristic of the wave has been altered when the grandmother reduces the volume.
(In the displacement-distance graph, Q is a crest and R is the point on the mean position directly below Q; P and S are points on the mean line.)

options.a: The length PS becomes more.
options.b: The length SR becomes less.
options.c: The length QR becomes less.
options.d: The length PR becomes less.

questions.solution: (c) The length QR becomes less. QR is the amplitude (crest height above the mean position). Lowering the volume reduces loudness, which means a smaller amplitude; the wavelength (related to PS/PR) is unchanged.
questions.figure_desc: Displacement-distance graph of a wave with points P, S, R on the mean line and Q at a crest above R.

questions.topic: Heat: heat capacity and specific heat capacity
questions.question:
Data: mass = 10 g, quantity of heat supplied = 120 J, rise in temperature = 10 °C.
STATEMENT A: The heat capacity of the substance is 12 J/g.
STATEMENT B: The specific heat capacity of the substance is 1.2 J/gK.

options.a: Only statement A is correct.
options.b: Only statement B is correct.
options.c: Both statements A and B are correct.
options.d: Both statements A and B are incorrect.

questions.solution: (b) Only statement B is correct. Heat capacity = Q/Δt = 120/10 = 12 J/K (not J/g), so A is wrong. Specific heat capacity = Q/(mΔt) = 120/(10 × 10) = 1.2 J g⁻¹ K⁻¹, so B is right.

questions.topic: Electricity: switch in neutral wire, household circuits
concepts: switch must be in live wire for safety
questions.question:
Assertion (A): A switch will serve the purpose of making and breaking a circuit when it is connected to the neutral wire.
Reason (R): Neutral wire is at zero potential.

options.a: Both Assertion and Reason are true, and the Reason is the correct explanation of the Assertion
options.b: Both Assertion and Reason are true, but Reason is not the correct explanation of the Assertion
options.c: Assertion is true, but the Reason is false.
options.d: Both Assertion & Reason are false.

questions.solution: (b) Both Assertion and Reason are true, but Reason is not the correct explanation of the Assertion. A switch in the neutral wire does still make and break the circuit (though it is unsafe, since the appliance stays connected to the live wire when off). The neutral wire is indeed at zero potential, but that does not explain why the switch can make/break the circuit.

questions.topic: Magnetism: polarity of electromagnets / solenoids
concepts: polarity of solenoid by clock rule
questions.question:
The given rods will attract each other when:
(Two identical soft-iron rods are placed end to end, each wound with an identical coil; the first coil has terminals A and B, the second C and D, in the same relative positions.)

options.a: A and C are connected to positive terminal of the battery.
options.b: B and C are connected to the positive terminal of the battery.
options.c: A and D are connected to the positive terminal of the battery.
options.d: A and D are connected to the negative terminal of the battery.

questions.solution: (a) A and C are connected to the positive terminal of the battery. The coils are wound identically, so connecting the corresponding terminals (A and C) to the positive terminal sends current the same way round both coils. Both rods then have the same pole orientation (N–S, N–S), so the facing ends are unlike poles and attract. In (c) and (d) the currents are opposite, so the facing ends are like poles and repel.
questions.figure_desc: Two soft-iron rods side by side, each wound with a coil; left coil leads A, B and right coil leads C, D.

questions.topic: Modern Physics: balancing nuclear equations
concepts: conservation of mass number and atomic number in decay
questions.question:
Which of the following equations are correctly balanced? (Notation: X(A, Z) means mass number A, atomic number Z.)
A. X(q−1, p−5) → Y(q−5, p−3) + He(4, 2)
B. Z(q−4, p−4) → X(q−4, p−5) + e(0, −1)
C. X(q−1, p−5) → Y(q−5, p−7) + He(4, 2)
D. Z(q−4, p−7) → X(q−4, p−5) + 2 e(0, −1)

options.a: Only D
options.b: Only C
options.c: Both A & B
options.d: Both C & D

questions.solution: (d) Both C & D. Check mass numbers and atomic numbers on both sides. C: q−1 = (q−5) + 4 and p−5 = (p−7) + 2 ✓. D: q−4 = (q−4) + 0 and p−7 = (p−5) + 2(−1) ✓. A fails on atomic number: (p−3) + 2 = p−1 ≠ p−5. B fails: (p−5) + (−1) = p−6 ≠ p−4.

questions.topic: Sound: resonance in air columns with tuning forks
concepts: shorter air column resonates at higher frequency
shorter fork prongs give higher frequency
questions.question: The picture shows three cylinders filled with water to a different extent (P has the least water, Q the most, R in between). The tuning forks L, M and N (L shortest prongs, N longest) in vibration produce louder sound when held above the mouth of the cylinders. Which combination is correct for hearing a louder sound of the tuning fork?

options.a: L – R, M – Q, N – P
options.b: L – P, M – Q, N – R
options.c: L – R, M – P, N – Q
options.d: L – Q, M – R, N – P

questions.solution: (d) L – Q, M – R, N – P. A louder sound is resonance: the fork's frequency matches the natural frequency of the air column. The shortest fork L has the highest frequency and needs the shortest air column (Q, most water). N has the lowest frequency and needs the longest air column (P, least water). M matches R.
questions.figure_desc: Three cylinders P, Q, R with increasing water levels (P lowest, Q highest) and three tuning forks L, M, N of increasing size.

questions.topic: Heat: thermal (heat) capacity
concepts: heat capacity = Q/Δt, independent of how mass is distributed
questions.question: Three metals, A, B and C, are supplied with the same quantity of heat. Their masses are in the ratio 2:3:4. If they show the same rise in the temperature, then the ratio of their thermal capacities will be:
questions.solution: (a) 1:1:1. Thermal capacity C' = Q/Δt. Q and Δt are the same for all three, so the thermal capacities are equal whatever the masses.

questions.topic: Electricity: resistance depends on length and diameter
questions.question: The diagram shows different copper conductors of diameters d and 2d and lengths which are multiples of l: A (diameter 2d, length l), B (diameter d, length 3l), C (diameter 2d, length 2l), D (diameter d, length l). The increasing order of their resistances will be:

options.a: A < B < C < D
options.b: A < C < D < B
options.c: A < D < C < B
options.d: D < A < C < B

questions.solution: (b) A < C < D < B. R = ρl/A ∝ l/d². A: l/4d² = 0.25; B: 3l/d² = 3; C: 2l/4d² = 0.5; D: l/d² = 1 (in units of ρl/d² up to a common factor). Order: A (0.25) < C (0.5) < D (1) < B (3).

questions.topic: Magnetism: magnetic effect of current
concepts: current-carrying wire produces a magnetic field
questions.question: A magnetic compass is present on a small table, very close to the wall in a room. A man enters the room and switches on the Air Conditioner fitted near the ceiling. He observes that the needle in the compass shows immediate deflection. Identify the most probable reason for the deflection.

options.a: Air blowing in the room.
options.b: Current starts flowing through AC wire concealed in the adjacent wall.
options.c: Vibrations are produced when the Man starts talking to his wife in the kitchen.
options.d: Vibrations were produced due to a file in his hand that fell on the ground.

questions.solution: (b) Current starts flowing through AC wire concealed in the adjacent wall. A current-carrying wire produces a magnetic field around it, which deflects the nearby compass needle.

questions.topic: Heat: specific heat capacity and temperature change
questions.question: Two substances, A and B, have the same mass. Substance A has a higher specific heat capacity than substance B. What consequences would you expect when these substances are subjected to the same amount of heat energy?

options.a: Substance A will experience a smaller temperature change than substance B.
options.b: Substance A will experience a larger temperature change than substance B.
options.c: Both substances will experience the same temperature change.
options.d: Either of them can show a greater change in temperature as the temperature change depends on factors other than specific heat capacity.

questions.solution: (a) Substance A will experience a smaller temperature change than substance B. Δt = Q/(mc); with Q and m equal, a larger c gives a smaller Δt.

questions.topic: Light: refraction through a prism
concepts: at emergence angle of refraction > angle of incidence
questions.question:
A student traces the path of a ray of light through a glass prism for different angles of incidence. He analyses each diagram and draws the following conclusion:
I. On entering the prism, the light ray bends towards its base.
II. Light ray suffers refraction at the point of incidence and at the point of emergence while passing through the prism.
III. An emergent ray bends at a certain angle to the direction of the incident ray.
IV. While emerging from the prism at the second surface, the angle of refraction is less than the angle of incidence at that surface.
Which of the above inferences are correct?

options.a: I, II and III
options.b: I, III and IV
options.c: II, III and IV
options.d: All of these.

questions.solution: (a) I, II and III. IV is wrong: at the second surface light goes from glass (denser) to air (rarer), so it bends away from the normal and the angle of refraction (emergence) is greater than the angle of incidence there.

questions.chapter: Force: Turning Forces and Uniform Circular Motion
questions.topic: Force, Work, Power and Energy: uniform circular motion - tangential velocity
questions.question: A metal ball is whirled inside a ring placed on a table, as shown in the diagram P (the ball goes round so that it moves to the right along the far side of the ring and to the left along the near side). The diagram Q shows the motion of the ball after the ring is lifted: it moves off in a straight line to the right. Which of the following diagrams shows the correct position of the metal ball in the ring when the ring is lifted?

options.a: Ball at the near (front) edge of the ring
options.b: Ball at the left edge of the ring
options.c: Ball at the far (back) edge of the ring
options.d: Ball at the right edge of the ring

questions.solution: (c) The ball at the far (back) edge of the ring. When the ring is lifted, the centripetal force vanishes and the ball moves along the tangent in the direction of its instantaneous velocity. It moves off to the right, and only on the far side of the ring is the ball moving to the right.
questions.figure_desc: Diagram P: ring on a table with the ball and an arrow showing its sense of rotation; Q: ball moving off to the right; options (a)-(d) show the ball at different positions on the ring.

questions.topic: Light: scattering - reddish evening sky
questions.question:
Assertion (A): Sometimes the sky appears reddish in the evening.
Reason (R): Red, being longer in wavelength, scatter more than the other colours.

options.a: A and R are true, and R is the reason for A.
options.b: A and R are true, and R is not the reason for A.
options.c: A is true, but R is false.
options.d: A is false, but R is true.

questions.solution: (c) A is true, but R is false. At sunset light travels a long path through the atmosphere; shorter wavelengths are scattered away and red, which scatters least (scattering ∝ 1/λ⁴), reaches the eye. R is false because red scatters the least.

questions.topic: Force, Work, Power and Energy: zero work
questions.question:
Assertion (A): When the displacement is zero, then the work is zero. So, if the work done is zero, then it necessarily means the displacement is zero.
Reason (R): Work done is calculated by the relation W = F S cos θ.

options.a: A and R are true, and R is the reason for A.
options.b: A and R are true, and R is not the reason for A.
options.c: A is true, but R is false.
options.d: A is false, but R is true.

questions.solution: (d) A is false, but R is true. W = F s cos θ is zero also when θ = 90° (force perpendicular to displacement, e.g. circular motion), even though s ≠ 0. So zero work does not necessarily mean zero displacement.

questions.topic: Force, Work, Power and Energy (as printed): frequency of a stretched string
questions.question: Which of the following statement is CORRECT? The frequency of a stretched string is:

options.a: directly proportional to its length but inversely proportional to the tension of the wire.
options.b: inversely proportional to its length but directly proportional to the tension of the wire.
options.c: directly proportional to the square root of its length but inversely proportional to the tension of the wire.
options.d: inversely proportional to its length but directly proportional to the square root of the tension of the wire.

questions.solution: (d) inversely proportional to its length but directly proportional to the square root of the tension of the wire. f = (1/2l)√(T/m).

questions.topic: Light: refraction from rarer to denser medium
concepts: rarer to denser bends towards normal
questions.question: A ray of light passes obliquely from an optical medium of refractive index 1.33 to another medium of refractive index 1.5. While passing from the first medium to the second, the light ray will:

options.a: bend towards the normal.
options.b: bend away from the normal.
options.c: move along the normal.
options.d: suffer total internal reflection.

questions.solution: (a) bend towards the normal. It goes from an optically rarer (1.33) to a denser (1.5) medium, so it slows down and bends towards the normal; total internal reflection is possible only from denser to rarer.

questions.topic: Heat: latent heat of fusion of ice
concepts: high specific latent heat of fusion of ice
questions.question: Rivers which originate from the glaciers at high altitudes have a supply of water throughout the year. This is because ice in high mountains does not melt all at once. This is due to:

options.a: high specific heat of ice.
options.b: low specific heat of ice.
options.c: low specific latent heat of fusion of ice.
options.d: high specific latent heat of fusion of ice.

questions.solution: (d) high specific latent heat of fusion of ice. Each gram of ice needs 336 J to melt with no change in temperature, so glaciers melt slowly and steadily.

questions.topic: Electricity: current in series combination
concepts: same current through resistors in series
questions.question: If three resistors R1, R2 and R3 are connected in series and R1 > R2 > R3, then what is the relation between the currents I1, I2 and I3 respectively flowing through them?
questions.solution: (a) I1 = I2 = I3. In a series circuit there is only one path, so the same current flows through every resistor regardless of its value.

questions.topic: Sound: stationary waves on a string - wavelength from loops
questions.question: Three strings P, Q and R of the same length vibrate in stationary-wave patterns: P shows 3 loops, Q shows 2 loops and R shows 1 loop. What is the ratio of wavelengths between P, Q and R?
questions.solution: (d) 2:3:6. Each loop is half a wavelength. For length L: P: 3(λ/2) = L ⇒ λ = 2L/3; Q: λ = L; R: λ = 2L. Ratio 2L/3 : L : 2L = 2 : 3 : 6.
questions.figure_desc: Three strings of equal length vibrating with 3 loops (P), 2 loops (Q) and 1 loop (R).

questions.topic: Heat: change of state - molecular energy
concepts: latent heat increases potential energy of molecules
questions.question: During the change of state of a substance from solid to liquid, heat is absorbed by a body, but its temperature does not rise. Which of the following statements explains the phenomenon?

options.a: Only K.E of the molecules increases, but P.E remains the same.
options.b: Only P.E of the molecules increases, but K.E remains the same.
options.c: Both K.E and P.E of the molecules increase.
options.d: There is no increase in the P.E and K.E of the molecules.

questions.solution: (b) Only P.E of the molecules increases, but K.E remains the same. The heat absorbed (latent heat) is used to overcome intermolecular forces (increasing separation, i.e. potential energy); temperature, a measure of average K.E., stays constant.

questions.topic: Magnetism: magnetic effect of current vs electromagnetic induction
questions.question:
Assertion (A): When current is passed through a wire, a magnetic field is generated around the wire.
Reason (R): Whenever there is a change of magnetic flux linked up with the coil, the induced current is generated in the coil.

options.a: Both A and R are correct, and R is the correct explanation of A.
options.b: Both A and R are correct, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
options.c: A is correct but R is wrong.
options.d: Both A and R are wrong.

questions.solution: (b) Both A and R are correct, but R is not the correct explanation of A. A describes the magnetic effect of current (Oersted); R states Faraday's law of electromagnetic induction, a different phenomenon.

questions.topic: Modern Physics: charges on particles
questions.question: Which of the following combinations correctly shows the charges on the particles? (Columns: +1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹ C | −1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹ C | +3.2 × 10⁻¹⁹ C)

options.a: proton | neutron | alpha particle
options.b: alpha particle | electron | neutron
options.c: proton | electron | alpha particle
options.d: electron | proton | alpha particle

questions.solution: (c) proton, electron, alpha particle. A proton carries +1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹ C, an electron −1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹ C and an alpha particle (2 protons + 2 neutrons) +3.2 × 10⁻¹⁹ C; a neutron is uncharged.

questions.chapter: Force: Turning Forces and Uniform Circular Motion
questions.topic: Force, Work, Power and Energy: centre of gravity - sphere vs cone, filled vs empty
concepts: C.G. of sphere at its centre
C.G. of solid cone h/4, hollow cone h/3 from base
questions.question: Anu and Amy purchased ice creams in plastic balls and cones, respectively, during their outing at the science fair. After consuming their ice creams, Anu stated that regardless of whether they were filled with ice cream or empty, the centre of gravity of the objects would remain unchanged. Do you agree with Anu? Why?
questions.solution: No, I do not fully agree. For the spherical plastic ball, the C.G. stays at the geometric centre whether it is filled or empty, because the mass is distributed symmetrically about the centre in both cases. For the cone, the C.G. changes: a filled (solid) cone has its C.G. at h/4 from the base, while an empty (hollow) cone has its C.G. at h/3 from the base. So Anu's statement holds only for the ball.

marking_points.point: States 'No' and that the C.G. of the sphere stays at its centre whether filled or empty
C.G. of the cone shifts: h/4 from base when filled (solid) vs h/3 from base when empty (hollow)

questions.chapter: Force: Turning Forces and Uniform Circular Motion
questions.topic: Force, Work, Power and Energy: torque due to weight
concepts: weight produces a moment about the point of support
questions.question:
The picture shows a boy climbing a rope ladder hanging from the branch of a tree. The boy finds it difficult to climb the ladder as it turns about the axis where he is holding. The instructor tells the boy to stretch the body with the hands stretched up and make the body parallel to the ladder and climb.
(a) Which force caused the ladder to turn?
questions.solution: The boy's own weight (gravitational force) acting through his centre of gravity, which lies away from the line of the ladder, produces a moment (torque) about the point where he holds the ladder, so the ladder turns.

marking_points.point: The boy's weight acting at his C.G., at a distance from the ladder, produces a turning moment about his grip

questions.chapter: Force: Turning Forces and Uniform Circular Motion
questions.topic: Force, Work, Power and Energy: reducing moment arm
questions.question:
The picture shows a boy climbing a rope ladder hanging from the branch of a tree. The boy finds it difficult to climb the ladder as it turns about the axis where he is holding. The instructor tells the boy to stretch the body with the hands stretched up and make the body parallel to the ladder and climb.
(b) How does keeping the body parallel to the ladder make climbing easier?
questions.solution: Keeping the body stretched and parallel to the ladder brings the line of action of his weight close to the ladder, so the perpendicular distance (moment arm) from the axis is nearly zero. The turning moment (weight × perpendicular distance) becomes very small, so the ladder does not twist and climbing is easier.

Regenerative braking involves harnessing the energy that is typically lost when a car decelerates and brakes and instead using it to recharge the car's batteries. Unlike traditional braking systems that simply dissipate energy, regenerative braking allows some of that energy to be recycled.
(a) What is the energy conversion process that results in the wastage of energy in a normal car during braking?
questions.solution: In normal braking, the kinetic energy of the car is converted into heat energy (and some sound) by friction between the brake pads and the wheels/discs; this heat is lost to the surroundings.

questions.topic: Sound: loudness depends on area of vibrating surface

questions.question:

Door opened: tumbrel displaced, its weight gets a moment arm and produces a restoring torque that closes the door

questions.topic: Force, Work, Power and Energy: conservation of mechanical energy in a pendulum
questions.question:
Two students are conducting experiments with identical 100 g mass simple pendulums, each raising the bob 5 m above the mean position. Graphs of velocity against position (from extreme position through the mean position to the other extreme) show that the maximum velocity at the mean position is 10 m/s for student 1 and 8 m/s for student 2. questions.solution: P.E. at the extreme position: U = mgh = 0.1 × 10 × 5 = 5 J. K.E. at the mean position for student 1: K = ½mv² = ½ × 0.1 × 10² = 5 J. U = K, so no energy is lost; the motion of student 1's pendulum is free of friction.

marking_points.point: K = ½ × 0.1 × 10² = 5 J = U, so no loss to friction

questions.solution: No. For student 2, K.E. at the mean position = ½ × 0.1 × 8² = 3.2 J, less than the 5 J of P.E. Total energy is still conserved, so there is no violation of the law of conservation of energy.

questions.topic: Heat: slope of heating curve and specific heat capacity
